newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Rwanda must respect Zaire's borders, Belgium says.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda must respect Zaire's borders, Belgium says.

text.p: Belgium, using its influence as former colonial ruler, on Monday called on Rwanda to respect Zaire's borders and asked for Rwanda's help in getting aid to the more than one million refugees in war-ravaged eastern Zaire.
"Our first message to Rwanda is that it must respect Zaire's territory," said Belgian Foreign Minister Erik Derycke after a meeting with his Rwandan counterpart Anastase Gasana.

"This is not the time to rediscuss African borders set out at the Berlin Conference," Derycke said, referring to an 1885 conference of European colonial powers which formed the basis for Zaire and Rwanda's present borders.

Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu -- while denying that Rwanda has territorial ambitions in eastern Zaire -- called last week for a "second Berlin Conference which should reflect on the consequences of the present borders."

Derycke also said Gasana denied Rwandan soldiers were active on Zairean territory. Zaire has repeatedly said that soldiers of the Rwandan Tutsi-led army have lent support to the Zairean ethnic Tutsi rebels who are reported to have seized several eastern Zairean border towns.

Gasana told Belgian television earlier today the Belgian government should put pressure on Zaire to enter dialogue with Rwanda. Zaire refuses talks with Rwanda as long as Rwandan troops are on its territory.
Derycke said Belgium could not ascertain whether or not Rwandan troops were in Zaire. But he added Belgium would continue to act as mediator between its two former colonies.
He added that he had asked Rwanda to help establish "humanitarian corridors" to bring aid to the Rwandan refugees in Zaire and through which they could return home.
Derycke said Belgium believed these corridors should have military protection if they must serve as refugee passageways.

He reiterated Belgium would not consider sending troops to help establish these corridors. "We can only give financial or logistical support. It would not be adequate for Belgian soldiers to start a mission in a former colonial territory."
Earlier today, France and Spain proposed a multi-national force to guarantee distribution of aid to the refugees.
Derycke said Rwanda should welcome its refugees back, but questioned whether the Tutsi-led regime was willing to do that. "They say they do, but we see no practical proof of that."
The more than one million Rwandans who have been stuck in camps in eastern Zaire for two years are mainly of the majority Hutu tribe. They fled Rwanda after the minority Tutsis took power in 1994.

Belgian Secretary of State for Cooperation and Development Reginald Moreels, also present at the talks with Gasana, said Belgium had set aside 150 million Belgian francs ($4.81 million) for a humanitarian operation if and when it started. ($1=31.18 Belgian Franc)
